en: The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching to Hāritī, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Tanwulan of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Grove in Śrāvastī, teaching the Hāritī Ānanda.
Kātyāyana, accompanied by five hundred upāsakas, went to where Śāriputra was; having paid his respects, he withdrew to sit down.
Śāriputra preached the sūtra for them, and they departed with great joy.
He approached the Buddha once more, prostrated himself with his head to the ground, joined his palms, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to sit.
The Buddha asked Hakuō Anagāmin:
"By what merit have you been able to teach and transform these five hundred disciples so that they follow you?"
Kātyāyanāvavādaka immediately knelt with palms joined and said:
"I constantly practice the four matters taught by the Buddha.
What are these four?"
First, giving to others;
second, speaking what is wholesome;
third, attending to one's fellow students and providing for their needs, whether they have or lack anything.
"Fourth, one does not calculate when sharing wealth with fellow practitioners.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
The Buddhas of the past did not surpass these four matters;
the Buddhas of the future likewise will not surpass these four matters.
"The Buddhas of the present time likewise have no faults beyond these four matters.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra for Kātyāyana, they were all greatly delighted and withdrew.

Kātyāyanīputra returned home and entered his residence, where he called all the people, guests, and servants to sit before him. He skillfully expounded the sutras for them to provide understanding, speaking of the paths of birth and death, as well as good and evil.
He then ascended to the upper hall and called the treasury keepers and the female entertainers to sit before him, expounding the sutras and precepts for them; they were all filled with great joy.

He then ascended to the rear hall and, having finished expounding the sutras and precepts to the ladies and women, returned to the main hall. There, upon his seat for fasting and purification, he sat upright with a concentrated mind and immediately attained equanimity.

In the first heaven, the Four Heavenly Kings invited all the devas to assemble and sit together, and they collectively extolled the merits of Hāritī and Anāthapiṇḍada. From the most honored among the Four Heavenly Kings down to the abode of Hāritī and Anāthapiṇḍada, they praised the merits of Hāritī and Anāthapiṇḍada face-to-face.
When he was being exhorted by Ghoṣila Anāthapiṇḍika, he attained a state of equanimity and did not respond to the Heavenly King.
A certain bhikṣu who was at the Buddha’s side went to Ghoṣila Anāthapiṇḍika’s house. Upon seeing the bhikṣu, Ghoṣila Anāthapiṇḍika rose to welcome him and sat before him. The bhikṣu said:
"The Buddha has constantly praised your meritorious virtues in his midst."
Khaṇḍa-ānanda asked the bhikṣus,
"When the Buddha praised me, were there any laypeople present?
The bhikṣus replied:
"There are no white-robed laypeople.
Even if there were white-robed laypeople, what suspicion could there be?
He then rebuked Kātyāyanīputra, saying:
“The Buddha’s words are most sincere; I fear that those laypeople who do not believe them will fall into hell.
Even those who do believe the Buddha’s words would come to serve me and make offerings to me, yet I do not delight in troubling people; it is for this reason that I ask.”
The bhikṣu took his leave.
Kātyāyanīputra said to him, "I suspect you have not yet eaten since morning; please stay for a while and partake of some food."
He then served water for washing and presented the food.
When the meal was finished, the bhikṣu returned and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have just been to the house of Kātyāyanīputra, where he spoke these words on the way:"
"Among those seated before the Buddha, there was great mutual praise. Kātyāyana then asked me:
'When the Buddha praised me, were there any laypeople present?'"
I said: "There are no laypeople.
Even if there were laypeople, what kind of suspicion would there be?"
He said to Kātyāyanīputra, "The Buddha’s praise of me is indeed sincere and not false. Those laypeople who do not believe the Buddha’s words shall fall into hell;
even those who do believe them will come to serve me. I do not delight in troubling others, and it is for this reason that I asked."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent! Excellent!"
I have not always taught you all that there are seven matters concerning the *akopya-ānañjā* (the unshakable state); now I add one more matter, making them eight.
What are these eight matters?
First, one does not seek it, desiring that others not know of it;
second, one has faith, desiring that others not know of it;
third, one is personally ashamed, desiring that others not know of it.
Fourth, one feels shame within oneself and does not wish for others to know;
fifth, one practices with diligence and does not wish for others to know;
sixth, one observes oneself and does not wish for others to know.
Seventh, having attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not wish for others to know it;
eighth, being possessed of wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not wish for others to know it.
The reason one does not wish for others to know these is that one does not wish to disturb or trouble others; therefore, one does not wish for others to know them.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the bhikṣus were greatly rejoiced; they rose, came forward, and paid homage to the Buddha.
This concludes the *Heshao Anagamin Sutra* spoken by the Buddha.
